activities.anchor: a machine needs the initial value of the total, the order of iteration, and what to do at the last item
activities.caption: pair each construct with the capability it adds
activities.name: progConstructsMatch

config.prompt: Pair each construct with the capability it adds:

pairs.right: hold a number under a name for later
wrap steps under a callable name

config.why: Every other language is a dialect with different punctuation — the constructs are the vocabulary.

activities.anchor: a beginner's first runtime error, and a permanent professional reflex
activities.caption: find the faulty line — a beginner's type notes
activities.name: progTypesSpot

config.prompt: One line of these type notes is wrong — click it:
lines: age = 17 stores 17 under the name age; every later mention fetches the current binding.
MAX_SPEED written once in capitals documents intent and lets a change happen in exactly one place.
In Python, "5" + 3 is "53" — string concatenation, same as JavaScript.
Every input from a keyboard or file arrives as text, so 'read a number' means 'read text, then cast it'.
config.correction: In Python, "5" + 3 raises a TypeError — the concatenation answer is JavaScript's behaviour; same symbols, different type logic.
config.why: Which operations make sense is decided by the data's kind — the genre of bug that knowing it prevents.

activities.anchor: In code it is an action
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the equals sign, twice
activities.name: progAssignPredict

config.q: x = 5 is followed by x = 6. In a program, this is:
choices: Ordinary — the symbol performs an assignment: compute the right side, bind it to the name
A contradiction — a variable can only be assigned once
A syntax error in every language
Legal only in mathematics, never in code
config.why: The mathematical equals and the programming equals share a symbol and nothing else — so count = count + 1 is legal and ordinary.

activities.anchor: the natural pair with input ("keep asking until valid") and with files ("until end of file")
activities.caption: fill the blanks — selection and iteration's classic bugs
activities.name: progControlCloze

config.text: Selection conditions are boolean expressions — comparisons joined by %%0%% — and the classic bugs are %%1%% bugs: greater-than versus greater-or-equal at exactly the pass mark. Count-controlled loops run a known number of times; %%2%%-controlled loops keep going as long as their condition holds, stopping the moment it flips. An infinite loop's usual cause is the missing %%3%% line.
config.hint: Exactly-50 belongs in the test data; a never-flipping condition has no line that changes anything.

activities.anchor: Two-dimensional arrays extend the idea to grids
activities.caption: call the size of the rainfall grid
activities.name: progRainEst

config.prompt: A rainfall table holds 52 weeks by 7 days — how many individual values?
config.why: 52 × 7 = 364 cells; summing one week is the inner pass, and the whole year wraps it in the outer weeks pass.
config.context: Outer walking weeks, inner walking days — nesting composed.

activities.anchor: the difference between a report and a log, and a classic exam question
activities.caption: from results.csv to an average — the pipeline
activities.name: progFileOrder

config.prompt: From results.csv to a total — put the pipeline in order:
items: Open in read mode — name the path and the mode
Split each line on its commas into fields
Cast the third field to a number
Accumulate the total and the count
Close — or let a with-block close it for you
config.why: Read, split, cast, total — the standard process-a-data-file algorithm the data-science strand will industrialise.

activities.anchor: The craft is the composition, not the vocabulary.
activities.caption: the finished program meets boundary data
activities.name: progBoundaryBranch

config.root: The temperature report is written. Now attack it with boundary data.

start.text: Test: n = 0 — the user enters zero values.

choices.label: The average divides by the count — count is zero, the program crashes
choices.feedback: Exactly the boundary case: guard the division and report 'no data' instead.

choices.label: Skip the test — zero values is not a real scenario
choices.feedback: Empty input is the case least expected and most shipped; boundary and erroneous data exist precisely for it.

skip.text: The demo impresses until the first empty file — test what the program should reject, not just what it accepts.

guard.text: Guarded. Next test: all values equal.

choices.label: Max, min and average come out identical — is that a bug?
choices.feedback: Not a bug: for [7, 7, 7] the honest report is 7, 7, 7 — the boundary test proves the seed logic assumes no variety.

choices.label: Refuse repeated values so max ≠ min
choices.feedback: That invents a rule the spec never had — the spec says report, not deduplicate.

equal.text: Boundary data's job: prove the logic at the edges — a single value, all equal, zero values, and a letter at the prompt.

refuse.text: The spec is the contract — amendments change the spec first, then the code.

config.why: Every test maps to a data class; the assembly — not the constructs — is the skill.
